input: Draft a house emergency exit plan with kids

keyUnknowns.whyItMatters: The number, ages, and needs of children drastically change the plan — a toddler requires carrying and assigned adult responsibility, while a teen can self-evacuate or assist.
The plan could cover fire only, or a broader set of emergencies (gas leak, earthquake, intruder) — each requires different exit logic and meeting points.
The home's layout (single-story vs. multi-story, apartment vs. house) directly determines which exit routes are possible and whether window ladders or stairwell plans are needed.
The desired output format — a printed poster, a simple checklist, a step-by-step document, or a drawn floor map — determines how the plan should be structured.
Any mobility limitations, medical needs, or pets that must be included will constrain exit routes and responsibilities and must be planned around explicitly.
Whether the plan needs to be child-readable and independently actionable by the kids, or is primarily a reference for adults, changes language, complexity, and visual design.
Some families want a drill-ready, rehearsal-focused plan with assigned roles and timed steps; others want a simple, calm reference guide — the tone and depth differ significantly.

gold.taskTitle: Draft a family emergency exit plan with kids
gold.taskDescription: Create a practical, household-specific emergency exit plan that accounts for the presence of children.

questions.title: How old are the children who need to be included?
questions.description: Ages determine whether children can self-evacuate, need to be carried, or can take on helper roles in the plan.

questions.title: Which emergencies should this plan cover?
questions.description: Clarifies whether the plan is fire-only or should include other scenarios like gas leaks, earthquakes, or intruders.

questions.title: What type and layout of home do you live in?
questions.description: Single-story house, multi-story house, or apartment building each require fundamentally different exit route planning.

questions.title: What format should the final plan be in?
questions.description: Options include a printed poster, a floor map with routes drawn, a written checklist, or a digital document.

questions.title: Are there any mobility needs, medical conditions, or pets to plan around?
questions.description: Special needs or pets add constraints to exit routes and require assigned responsibilities in the plan.

questions.title: Should the children be able to follow the plan independently?
questions.description: Determines whether the plan must use child-friendly language, visuals, and steps kids can execute on their own.

questions.title: Should the plan include drills and assigned roles for each person?
questions.description: Some families want a rehearsal-focused, role-based plan; others prefer a simple general reference guide.
